# Jhāna Saṁyutta (SN 34)

**ID:** SN 34
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Jhāna Saṁyutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Linked Discourses on Absorption
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/sn34
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0303m.mul12.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Jhānasaṁyutta* (SN 34), also known as the *Samādhisaṁyutta*, is the thirty-fourth collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated as Chapter XIII in the *Khandhavagga* [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 2003_x]. Unlike the second *Jhānasaṁyutta* found in the *Mahāvagga* (SN 53), which treats the four jhānas as meditative attainments, SN 34 focuses not on meditative states as such, but rather on the technical process of meditation and the specific faculties required for success in concentration (*samādhi*), leading Bhikkhu Bodhi to suggest that an earlier designation may have been *Jhāyanasaṁyutta* [Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 2003_x]. The collection comprises 55 discourses examining various proficiencies of the meditator, including skill in entering immersion, maintaining it, emerging from it, skill regarding its support (*ārammaṇa*), and its domain (*gocara*) [SuttaCentral; Sujato; Sujato 2012].

Structurally, the collection is constructed as a comprehensive combinatorial "wheel" (*cakka*) that pairs meditative skills dyadically across all possibilities [Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 2003_x]. Each pair of qualities is analyzed through a fourfold matrix: a practitioner who possesses the first skill but not the second, one who possesses the second but not the first, one who possesses neither, and one who possesses both [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003_x]. In every discourse, the meditator who has perfected both skills is pronounced the foremost and most excellent [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003_x]. The text is commented upon in the *Sāratthappakāsinī* (Spk), the commentary to the *Saṁyuttanikāya* [Bodhi 2003_x].

According to SuttaCentral, the entire collection of 55 suttas corresponds to a single parallel in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama*, SĀ 883 (四種禪) [SuttaCentral]. In addition, DharmaNexus records extensive internal Pali text reuse across 75 texts, showing the highest volume of shared formulaic phrasing with the *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4), *Chakkanipāta* (AN 6), *Iddhipāda Saṁyutta* (SN 51), and the Abhidhamma's *Ñāṇavibhaṅga* (Vb 16) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns passages automatically with Tibetan canonical texts, such as the *Kalāpasūtravṛtti* (D4288) and Prajñāpāramitā treatises (D3787, D3807) [DharmaNexus].
